newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS-Australia fears drought could singe economy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Australia fears drought could singe economy.

text.p: The Australian government on Thursday expressed fears of a nation-wide drought and said dry weather could dent official forecasts for economic growth.
Treasurer Peter Costello sounded the warning in a speech to economists in Melbourne, prompting some in his audience to say that a full-blown drought posed the biggest risk to the economy.

"If we were to have a bad drought we could see GDP (gross domestic product) forecasts revised by anything between one and 1.5 percent," said Todd Ritchie, economist with the National Farmers' Federation.
The government has forecast economic growth to accelerate to 3.75 percent for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1998 -- below financial market expectations of around four percent growth.
Five cuts to official interest rates over the past 12 months, and improved prospects for world economic growth and commodity prices, have brightened Australia's economic outlook.
But on Thursday Costello cited growing signs of a strong El Nino weather pattern, usually associated in Australia with low rainfall, and evoked memories of the severe 1982/83 drought.
"Weather conditions data also indicated that the event is the strongest since the episode of 1982/83, a period of widespread drought in Australia," he said.
"Lower than forecast farm product would lead to lower GDP growth in 1997/98, but it is too early to change the forecast ...," he added.
The timing, distribution and amount of rainfall over the next month will be crucial in determining if official forecasts for farm output and economic growth can be met, Costello said.
Australia's farm sector accounts for roughly four percent of national GDP, with the national wheat crop looming as potentially the biggest economic casualty from another drought.
The wheat crop has just been planted and now needs good rainfall to guarantee a healthy crop, economists said.
"It's true that El Nino is the key risk (to economic growth)," said Access Economics chief economist Chris Richardson told Reuters.
"In the worst case, it could knock one percentage point off GDP, but that's a really worst-case scenario. Even then I would expect a GDP (growth) of three percent," he added.
Access Economics, a private economics consultancy, has forecast 3.9 percent economic growth in 1997/98.
Emphasising the doubts still surrounding the strength of Australia's economic acceleration, official data released on Thursday showed an unexpected drop in retail spending in June.
Retail trade fell 1.8 percent in June, against expectations of a 0.4 percent rise, official figures on Thursday showed. It was the third fall in the past four months.
Economists blamed unemployment, stuck above eight percent, for the weaker retail data.
